title: Where Bix Beiderbecke fits; Bix and Miles Davis
summary: Rose speculates that Bix would have gone modern like Miles Davis, had a love of melody, and might have drifted toward Coltrane. He also describes Davis as inarticulate. The third reel starts.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: As I say that, I begin to think of the numerous exceptions to it.

Well, one musician that I want to ask you about, which is, of course, my particular interest since I'm doing my dissertation on him, is Bix Beiderbeck. And maybe what I could ask you is, where would you fit Bix Beiderbeck into the history of jazz?

Well, I would say that in the first place, there is no fitting him into the history as such in a schematic sense. Fundamentally, it appeared from recorded evidence, it would appear that Bix, in a sense, shared the unique quality of Louis Armstrong, or would have shared it had he gotten old enough. To do so, as a musician of that highly personal quality, as to be able to transcend most of the groups and circumstances with which and in which he played. And he seemed to be an extraordinary individual artist. Now, plus, of course, the clear consideration that his impact and influence on the musicians of his time was so great that it would have been impossible to ignore. But I would think that Bix Beiderbeck's future development, had he lived, as would be indicated by the evidence of the tendencies that he already showed, would have been to, in the direction of a Miles Davis, for instance. I really feel that he would have gone along with every modern trend and every development that came out of the European modern composers and eventually would have...
Do you know, Al, do you have any idea where Miles Davis was influenced at all by the same kinds of things that Bix Beiderbeck was, for instance, Debussy or...

Well, Miles Davis is not a very articulate guy. And not only that, but he doesn't actually talk very much anyhow. So that he will say things like, you know, given a question, what is it that makes you decide what you're going to play when you get up on the stand? He says, well, I just think about it, and if it seems cool, I play it. Of course, that tells you nothing. And I found that he always tended to be very responsive to things that he had never heard before. Anytime he ever heard anything new that he had not heard before, he would show extreme interest. I also found that his enthusiasms flagged very rapidly. The second or third playing of a piece, for instance, would show him beginning to lose interest already because his head had already solved the harmonic structures.
Now, is there any comparison here to Beiderbeck, then?
I don't think so. I think that my impression is that from listening, that Beiderbeck had a genuine love of melody.
And that one, like Miles Davis, has no interest in melody at all.
Well, would Beiderbeck be playing bop, then, today, if he were alive?

I think he would have gravitated to that and possibly contributed to making some kind of sense out of it. I believe that he would have played bop during the period when it was popular. But I believe that he would have eventually drifted off into some non-objective area, which would have been of the Coltrane persuasion, rather than in any real organized way.
Wouldn't he have been closer to a more melodic lyrical player, like maybe Chet Baker?

Well, except for the fact that I believe that the lack of acceptance of that kind of music would have proven to be very discouraging to him. I believe that he would have been considered to be old hat and no longer of interest. I don't think that he would have survived as a favorite among the musicians. And I really do believe that that was necessary to him. I believe that he had to have sounding boards and he had to have... Okay. Okay, the third reel is on. Good.
